data communications: The exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium (the instructor's definition). A **data communications system** is a network of hardware and software that enables that exchange. See [What data communications is](#/comp3721-w1/data-communications).
telecommunication: Communication at a distance: telephony, telegraphy, and television. Plain **communication** is the exchange of information. See [What data communications is](#/comp3721-w1/data-communications).
jitter: Uneven delay in the delivery of audio or video packets. One of the four effectiveness characteristics with **delivery**, **accuracy** and **timeliness**. See [What data communications is](#/comp3721-w1/data-communications).
protocol: A set of rules that govern data communications; it represents an agreement between the communicating devices. Lecture 01b adds: it defines **what** is communicated, **how** and **when** (the format and order of messages and the actions taken). See [Five components](#/comp3721-w1/components-data-flow) and [Why we layer](#/comp3721-w1/why-layers).
simplex: Unidirectional data flow: one device only sends, the other only receives (mainframe to monitor, keyboard, TV). See [Data flow](#/comp3721-w1/components-data-flow).
half-duplex|half duplex: Two-directional communication, one direction at a time (walkie-talkie). See [Data flow](#/comp3721-w1/components-data-flow).
full-duplex|full duplex: Two-directional communication simultaneously (telephone). Signals in one direction share the capacity of the link with signals in the other direction. See [Data flow](#/comp3721-w1/components-data-flow).
node|nodes: An individual entity or point within a network (like a station). In a computer network a node is a **host / end system** or a **connecting device** (router, switch, modem). Links between nodes are the **edges**. See [Networks](#/comp3721-w1/networks).
host|end system: A device at the edge of the network that runs application programs: large computer, desktop, laptop, workstation, cellular phone. Hosts implement all five TCP/IP layers. See [Networks](#/comp3721-w1/networks).
throughput: How much data gets through per unit time. **Performance** is mainly measured in terms of throughput and delay. See [Networks](#/comp3721-w1/networks).
point-to-point: A dedicated link between two devices; the capacity of the link is reserved for those two (wire, microwave or satellite links). Contrast **multipoint**. See [Networks](#/comp3721-w1/networks).
multipoint|multidrop: More than two devices share a single link and its capacity, either **spatially shared** (simultaneously) or **timeshared** (taking turns). A bus topology is multipoint. See [Networks](#/comp3721-w1/networks).
topology: The geometric representation of the relationship of all the links and linking devices (nodes) to one another. Four basic ones: mesh, star, bus, ring. See [Topologies](#/comp3721-w1/topologies).
mesh: Every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device; $n$ devices need $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ links. Robust, private, easy fault isolation, but expensive and hard to install. See [Topologies](#/comp3721-w1/topologies).
star: Each device has a dedicated point-to-point link only to a central controller, usually called a **hub**; $n$ links for $n$ devices. Disadvantages: dependency on one single point, more cabling than bus and ring. See [Topologies](#/comp3721-w1/topologies).
bus: Multipoint topology: one long cable as a backbone with drop lines and taps; $n$ devices need 1 backbone + $n$ drop lines. Easy to install, hard to reconnect or isolate faults. See [Topologies](#/comp3721-w1/topologies).
ring: Each device has a dedicated point-to-point connection with only the two devices on either side (a repeater per device). Unidirectional traffic; a break can disable the whole network. See [Topologies](#/comp3721-w1/topologies).
hub: The central controller of a star topology. As a device (01c) it is a physical-layer **multiport repeater**: it repeats what it hears on one port out all other ports. See [Hubs, switches, routers](#/comp3721-w1/connecting-devices).
LAN: Local Area Network: usually privately owned, connects hosts in a single office, building or campus; limited in size; each host has a unique identifier; **WLAN** if wireless. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
WAN: Wide Area Network: a wider geographical span (town, state, country, world); interconnects switches, routers and modems; created and run by communication companies and leased by an organization. **Point-to-point WAN** connects two devices; **switched WAN** connects more than two and forms the backbone of global communication today. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
internet: Lower-case i: two or more networks that can communicate with each other (an internetwork). The **Internet** with capital I is the most notable internet, composed of thousands of interconnected networks. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
ARPANET: The Advanced Research Projects Agency Network, founded by the DoD; carried the first message ("LO") from UCLA on October 29, 1969. Its main design goal was **survivability**. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
access network: The network that physically connects an end system to the first router (edge router) on a path to any other distant end system. The **core network** is the routers, link-layer switches and links that interconnect end systems. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
ISP: Internet Service Provider. Customer networks connect to provider networks (national or regional ISPs), which connect to backbones (international ISPs) at **peering points**. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
DSL: Digital Subscriber Line, a telephone-network access method whose line can be used simultaneously for both voice and data. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
IETF: Internet Engineering Task Force: the organization that creates and publishes Internet standards and RFCs. Standards exist for **interoperability**. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
RFC: Request for Comment: a numbered, technical and detailed document defining standards, protocols, procedures and technologies for the Internet, published by the IETF. RFC-1 was written in 1969. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
Internet standard: A thoroughly tested specification and a formalized regulation that must be followed by those who work with the Internet; created and published by the IETF. See [LAN, WAN, Internet](#/comp3721-w1/lan-wan-internet).
service model: The services that a layer offers to the layer above it. Each layer provides its service by performing actions within that layer and by using the services of the layer directly below. See [Why we layer](#/comp3721-w1/why-layers).
protocol suite|protocol stack: A set of protocols organized in different layers, designed to work together. The **TCP/IP protocol suite** (five layers) is the Internet protocol stack; the **OSI model** (seven layers) is the ISO standard. See [TCP/IP and OSI](#/comp3721-w1/tcpip-osi).
PDU: Protocol Data Unit: a unit of data passed between layers of a protocol stack. Application **message**, transport **segment / user datagram**, network **datagram / packet**, data-link **frame**, physical **bits**. See [TCP/IP and OSI](#/comp3721-w1/tcpip-osi).
frame: The data-link layer PDU: the datagram plus a link header $H_L$ carrying link-layer (MAC) addresses for one link. The example on the slide is an Ethernet frame (64–1522 bytes). See [Encapsulation](#/comp3721-w1/encapsulation-addressing).
datagram|packet: The network layer PDU: the segment plus a network header $H_N$ carrying the source and destination IP (logical) addresses. See [Encapsulation](#/comp3721-w1/encapsulation-addressing).
segment|user datagram: The transport layer PDU (segment for TCP, user datagram for UDP): the message plus a transport header $H_T$ carrying port numbers. See [Encapsulation](#/comp3721-w1/encapsulation-addressing).
encapsulation: Adding a header at each layer on the way down the stack at the source: message → segment → datagram → frame → bits. **Decapsulation** removes them on the way up at the destination. See [Encapsulation](#/comp3721-w1/encapsulation-addressing).
NIC: Network Interface Card: where the physical and data-link layers are typically implemented; it handles communication over one specific link. See [TCP/IP and OSI](#/comp3721-w1/tcpip-osi).
TCP: Transmission Control Protocol, a transport-layer protocol (with UDP and SCTP) providing process-to-process delivery; its PDU is the segment. Transport protocols are almost always software in the end systems. See [TCP/IP and OSI](#/comp3721-w1/tcpip-osi).
UDP: User Datagram Protocol, a transport-layer protocol whose PDU is the user datagram. See [TCP/IP and OSI](#/comp3721-w1/tcpip-osi).
IP: Internet Protocol, the network-layer protocol (the network layer is also called the IP layer) that routes datagrams from source host to destination host using logical (IP) addresses. See [TCP/IP and OSI](#/comp3721-w1/tcpip-osi).
MAC address|link-layer address: The data-link (link-layer, physical) address that defines a specific host or router in a network (LAN or WAN). Switches filter on it; routers replace it on every hop. See [Encapsulation](#/comp3721-w1/encapsulation-addressing).
port number: The transport-layer address that identifies a process on a host. See [Encapsulation](#/comp3721-w1/encapsulation-addressing).
switch|link-layer switch: A connecting device operating in the physical and data-link layers: regenerates the signal and checks the MAC addresses in the frame, with **filtering** capability to pick the outgoing port (unlike a hub). Connects end systems together. See [Hubs, switches, routers](#/comp3721-w1/connecting-devices).
router: A connecting device operating in the physical, data-link and network layers; an **internetworking device** that connects networks. It has a MAC and an IP address per interface, acts only on frames addressed to the arriving interface, and changes both link-layer addresses when forwarding. See [Hubs, switches, routers](#/comp3721-w1/connecting-devices).
modem: Modulator-demodulator: a connecting device that changes the form of data (E01 exercise 3). See [Hubs, switches, routers](#/comp3721-w1/connecting-devices).
log|logarithm: The exponent to which the base must be raised to obtain a number: $\log_{b} a = c$ means $b^{c} = a$. No base written means base 10 ($\log 100 = 2$); $\log_{2} 32 = 5$. See [Math review](#/comp3721-w1/math-review).
